prompt.context: Your client is a private equity firm that has recently purchased a plastic materials manufacturer that makes products such as plastic soda bottles. The client is looking to cash out of their investment within 5 years and wants you to help improve the profitability of the manufacturer.
prompt.question: How would you improve the profitability of the manufacturer so the PE firm can maximize its return within a 5-year exit horizon?

clarifying_info.q: What products does the firm manufacture?
clarifying_info.a: Two types: plastic bottles (sold to large bottlers like Coke or Pepsi) and non-bottling goods (such as advertising displays for stores, sold directly to establishments like gas stations).

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of the bottling market?
clarifying_info.a: Can be calculated from revenues. The bottling market is growing at 10% per year in North America; the firm has 30% market share.

clarifying_info.q: How fast is the firm growing?
clarifying_info.a: The firm's bottling sales have been growing at 15% per year, projected 15% growth for each of the next two years.

clarifying_info.q: What plants does the firm have?
clarifying_info.a: Two plants: one in the southeast US that manufactures only bottles with capacity of 1.5B bottles; one in Canada that can produce both bottles and non-bottling materials with capacity of 500M products, currently producing non-bottling goods.

clarifying_info.q: What are the revenue and cost figures?
clarifying_info.a: Bottles sell for 5 cents each. Non-bottling generates $20M in revenues. Bottle costs: COGS (plastic) 2 cents/bottle, machinery 1 cent/bottle, labor 0.5 cent/bottle. Non-bottling has total variable costs of $18M. SG&A across the entire firm is $20M.
Yes, no downtime — plants are fully utilized. Plants use new, highly efficient machinery.
Yes, bottles are made to spec; non-bottling goods are not.

clarifying_info.q: Does the firm have a cost advantage?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the firm has higher quality products and manufactures at lower costs due to more efficient machinery.

framework: Revenues: analyze revenue streams for bottles vs. non-bottling (price per unit, volume, market share, growth trajectory)
Costs: break down variable costs (COGS, machinery, labor) and fixed costs (SG&A) for each product line
Capacity & Operations: assess current capacity utilization, constraints, and potential for reallocation
Profitability Comparison: calculate and compare profit margins for bottles vs. non-bottling to identify higher-value product
Strategic Options: evaluate converting Canada plant to bottling, risks of conversion, market share needed to sustain growth
Exit Fit: assess how any strategic change fits within the 5-year PE exit horizon

questions.prompt: Compare the profitability of the two products (bottling vs. non-bottling). Which has higher margins?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total revenues, total variable costs, total profit, and profit margin for each product line using the given figures. Key takeaway: bottling has significantly higher profit margins (30%) than non-bottling (10%).

math.setup: Bottling: capacity = 1.5B bottles; revenue = 5 cents/bottle; variable cost = 2+1+0.5 = 3.5 cents/bottle; profit per bottle = 1.5 cents. Non-bottling: revenue = $20M; variable cost = $18M.
math.answer: Bottling profit = $22.5M (30% margin); Non-bottling profit = $2M (10% margin). Bottling is significantly more profitable.

questions.prompt: Should the firm convert non-bottling production in the Canada plant to bottling? The conversion costs $3M. Assume the firm has sufficient cash. What is the projected profit from conversion and when does it break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use the previously calculated profit per bottle (1.5 cents) applied to the Canada plant's 500M unit capacity. Compare incremental profit to conversion cost to find breakeven. Key takeaway: conversion could add $7.5M in annual profit; breakeven is within year 1.

math.setup: Additional capacity from Canada conversion = 500M bottles; profit per bottle = 1.5 cents (previously calculated); conversion cost = $3M one-time.
steps: Projected additional profit: 500M x $0.015 = $7.5M per year
Breakeven: $3M cost / $7.5M annual profit = 0.4 years — breakeven in year 1
Net gain vs. current non-bottling: $7.5M - $2M (current Canada profit) = $5.5M incremental annual profit
math.answer: Conversion adds $7.5M in annual profit vs. $2M currently ($5.5M incremental uplift). One-time cost of $3M is recovered within the first year. Breakeven is in year 1.

questions.prompt: What are some non-financial risks to consider before converting non-bottling production to bottling in the Canada plant?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm implementation, distribution, cost, and people risks. Strong candidates will organize risks into clear buckets.

questions.prompt: How much additional market share does the firm need to gain over the next 2 years to sell the extra bottles produced after converting the Canada plant?
questions.guidance: Candidate should first calculate current bottling market size from given data, then project firm sales and market size forward two years, and compute required market share each year. Key takeaway: gaining ~3% market share over 2 years appears feasible.

math.setup: Current firm bottle production = 1.5B; current market share = 30%; market growth = 10%/year; firm sales growth = 15%/year.
math.answer: The firm needs to grow market share from 30% to ~31.4% in year 1 and ~32.8% in year 2 — approximately 3% additional market share over 2 years, which appears feasible given the firm's superior cost position and quality.

brainstorming.prompt: What are non-financial risks to consider before converting the Canada plant from non-bottling to bottling production?

categories.name: Implementation
ideas: How much time will conversion take?
Does the firm need a phased approach to avoid production gaps?

categories.name: Distribution
ideas: Will the current distribution network need to change to reach bottling customers?
How will distribution centers scale up given the growth projections?

categories.name: Costs
ideas: Will there be additional costs beyond the one-time $3M conversion cost?
Will variable costs like labor change after conversion?
Any change in profit margins at the Canada plant?
Can the firm re-negotiate supplier contracts to reduce COGS?

categories.name: People & Labor
ideas: Will the firm need to hire new workers in Canada or retrain current workers?
Is there organized labor at the Canada plant? Could there be union resistance to the change?

recommendation: The manufacturer should convert the non-bottling production in the Canada plant to bottling, as bottling offers significantly better margins (30% vs. 10%)
The additional capacity is needed to match anticipated demand growth; the firm's sales will exceed current capacity by the end of year 2 at projected growth rates
The one-time conversion cost of $3M is recovered within the first year, generating $7.5M in annual profit — a strong return well within the 5-year PE exit window
risks: The market may not continue growing at 10% per year, or may enter a period of decline
It may be difficult for the company to continue growing faster than the market (15% vs. 10%)
The non-bottling market and firm's non-bottling sales might be growing at a faster rate (no information was given), so capital could potentially be better deployed there
next_steps: Consider adding another plant or expanding existing plants to keep pace with sales growth beyond year 2; any expansion should fit within the 5-year PE exit horizon
Explore renting additional capacity from other plants as a capital-light option that is easier to reverse if market conditions worsen
Negotiate with suppliers and customers to further improve profitability
Evaluate whether a price increase is feasible given the firm's higher quality; note that lost market share from a price increase may be difficult to recover within a 5-year horizon
